title: Kimi K3.1 Pro is REALLY BAD!
description:
Star PandaCode on GitHub: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode

https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll be testing Moonshot's new Kimi K3.1 Pro on all six KingBench 4 tasks, and I'll compare it with Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Haiku 5.5, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and the rest of my chart. I ran the whole benchmark through PandaCode, my fully open-source app for coding agents, which is tuned for Kimi Code, with six K3.1 workers running in parallel and a separate evaluator testing every project. We'll go through the emulator, the Docker alternative, the room designer, the keyboard app, Pokémon Red and the Fitbit app one by one, and then look at the final score, what the run actually cost and what the open weights mean. At the end, I'll tell you whether K3.1 Pro is worth using, because the launch blog's "almost Opus" story does not hold up in real projects.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot's post-trained K3 with a 1M context, a 2–3× faster Highspeed version, and open weights promised by November 4th.
📊 The launch blog claims 65.7% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, right next to Opus 5.5 at 66.4% and well ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 58.2%.
💻 I ran all six KingBench 4 tasks through PandaCode, which is fully open source and has a dedicated Kimi Code integration.
🧠 K3.1 scores 5.37 out of 10, sixth out of eleven, behind Opus, Astra, Sol, Argon and even Haiku 5.5.
✅ It is honest about what it didn't build, it blocked all 20 malicious images in the Docker task, and it speaks the real VIA protocol in the keyboard app.
⚠️ It built only the Game Boy part of the emulator, its Docker alternative has no build or networking, and Pokémon has broken levelling and a save-wiping title screen.
💸 The whole run cost about $31.88, compared with $7.40 for Haiku 5.5 and under $2 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.
🔍 Most of that bill is 110 million cached tokens that it re-reads on every step, not the code it writes.
🎯 Once the weights land, it will be the best-scoring open-weight model on my chart, ahead of DeepSeek Flash and GLM.
👍 Verdict: a good open model, not a frontier one, and on the API Haiku or DeepSeek Flash are the smarter picks for now.

description:

In this video, I'll review Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Google's fast, cheap model for everyday coding and agentic work, starting with its positioning, pricing, speed, and availability. I'll put it through the six KingBench 4 app builds and show what actually works, what breaks, and how it compares with Carbon, Argon, and the competition. Then I'll look at its cost and behavior, including the tests that pass while the app is still broken. I'll explain how I would use it as a worker under a stronger lead in PandaCode, my app for running coding agents as a team, and how that compares with Google's Antigravity Orchestrator. Finally, I'll give my take on whether Google is behind in the AI race and why Hydrogen needs an independent reviewer before you trust its finished work.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Gemini 4 Hydrogen is adapted from Carbon and built for quick execution in agentic workflows, with a free API tier.
📊 The six KingBench 4 scores are emulator 3.2, container runtime 3.0, room designer 6.6, QMK configurator 3.5, Pokémon Red 3.0, and Fitbit desktop 5.6.
🎯 Hydrogen totals 24.9 out of 60 (41.5%), ranking 14 out of 15 models, with only MiniMax M3.1 Flash below it.
⚠️ The container runtime fails to isolate the host on macOS, and the Pokémon quest test teleports past a ledge that blocks normal progress.
💸 All six builds cost $6.04 at list price, used about 13.1 million tokens, and finished as a batch in 31 minutes.
🧠 Hydrogen writes first and compiles later, fixes the build errors it encounters, and never gets stuck in a loop.
🔍 It viewed no screenshots across the six runs, and its checks missed major problems in the apps it declared finished.
👥 In PandaCode, I would give Hydrogen narrow worker assignments under a stronger architect and a reviewer who actually opens the app.
🔀 Google's Antigravity Orchestrator pairs Carbon with Hydrogen workers and verifiers, but I would use Hydrogen as the worker rather than the verifier.
✅ Google is behind in autonomous whole-app coding rather than the AI race overall, and Hydrogen is a fast, cheap worker whose claim that the job is verified needs an independent check.

title: Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk - Fully Tested): Is IT ACTUALLY The BEST OPEN MODEL!?
description:

Finally, I'll go over the permission-corrected score, why the retries don't count, and where I'd actually use this model.

--
Key Takeaways:

🧪 I ran the same eight KingBench 3 prompts in OpenCode through OpenRouter, one fresh folder per task, and scored the delivered result.
🛗 The elevator simulation works properly, with all five spawned riders delivered and no browser errors, for 9.5 out of 10.
⚠️ The default contact lens and counting sessions ended without a file or an answer, so both score zero.

title: I Built KingBench 4 (HARD): Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6 Astra vs Sol vs Haiku 5.5 vs GLM 5.3
description:
In this video, I'll put GPT 6.1 Sol and GPT 6 Astra through Codex, Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 through Claude Code, and GLM 5.3 through OpenCode against the same six projects: a Game Boy, DS and 3DS emulator, a Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a VIA alternative for QMK keyboards, a Pokémon Red recreation through the first gym, and a Fitbit desktop app with a Rust backend. I'll go through what each model built, where the apps broke, and how each one was scored out of ten under the same strict rubric. Then we'll look at the final chart across all six projects and at the tokens and API-equivalent cost behind them. Finally, I'll tell you which model I'd pick for which kind of project.

--
Key Takeaways:

🏆 Opus 5.5 finishes first at 57.8%, followed by GPT 6 Astra at 56.5%, GPT 6.1 Sol at 55.0%, Haiku 5.5 at 54.2% and GLM 5.3 at 45.8%.
🎮 Nobody delivers the complete emulator; Opus wins it at 3.7 because it actually runs two DS test programs, while the others stop at Game Boy.
📦 None of the Docker alternatives proves it is more efficient than Docker; Sol leads that task at 5.0 thanks to its image tooling.
🛋️ The room designer is the strongest task for everyone: Opus wins at 8.5, and Astra and Haiku tie for second at 8.3.
⌨️ Opus (7.5) and Haiku (6.7) implement real keyboard remapping, while Sol and Astra build polished local editors that can't remap a connected keyboard.
⚠️ Opus can beat Brock in its Pokémon game, but the START menu closes instantly, so you can't save the badge — it scores 3.0, and Astra wins Pokémon at 8.5.
🏃 Opus leads the Fitbit app at 7.4, but one unrelated resting heart-rate sample drops a workout's daily load to zero.
💸 On the same three projects, Haiku's estimated API cost is about 85% lower than Opus's, with an average score of 71.3% versus 78.0%.
🔍 The habit that explains the scores: follow the feature all the way through — change the key, beat the gym and reload, import data with a missing measurement.
✅ Opus is the strongest starting point across these tasks, Astra is my pick for the browser game, and Haiku is the one to try first when cost matters.

description:

In this video, I'll review Gemini 4 Neon, Google's new mid-tier coding model released on November 18 between Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon, starting with its quiet rollout, $3 and $15 pricing, 1M context window, four thinking levels, and hands-on behavior in Antigravity CLI. Then I'll run it through all six KingBench 4 one-prompt app builds — a Rust Game Boy, DS, and 3DS emulator, a Go Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a QMK VIA keyboard configurator, Pokémon Red, and a Rust Fitbit desktop app — showing what actually worked, what broke, and how it landed at #2 out of 18 models for just $20.36. Next, I'll break down its coding habits and blind spots across 108.7 minutes and show how I pair Neon with Hydrogen, Panda Router, and a 9 out of 10 Council gate inside PandaCode, our free open-source multi-agent desktop app. Finally, I'll compare Gemini 4 Neon head-to-head against GPT-6.2 Sol, GPT-6.2 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.2 and give my honest verdict on whether it is actually worth using.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Gemini 4 Neon launched quietly on November 18 at $3 per million input tokens, $15 output including thinking, and $0.15 automatic cache reads, with no free tier and no November intro discount.
🧠 On paper it offers a unified 1 million token window, 64,000 output tokens per hop, Long Decode up to 1 million, and four thinking levels up to extra high, spending 56% to 81% of output tokens on thinking with zero preamble yapping.
📊 Across the six KingBench 4 builds, Neon scored 4.3 on the Rust emulator, 3.0 on the Go container runtime, 8.5 on the 3D room designer, 6.2 on the QMK configurator, 8.4 on Pokémon Red, and 7.5 on the Fitbit desktop app.
🎯 Neon finishes with 37.9 out of 60 (63.2%), ranking #2 out of 18 models behind only Claude Fable 5.2 (42.0) and beating Claude Opus 5.5 (34.7), GPT-6.2 Astra (33.6), GPT-6.1 Sol (33.0), Argon (32.6), Carbon (32.0), GPT-6.2 Sol (29.6), and Hydrogen (24.9).
💸 The entire six-app run used 27.1 million tokens for $20.36 at list prices, nearly 11 times cheaper than Fable 5.2 ($222) and cheaper than both GPT-6.2 Astra ($27.93) and Carbon ($23.04 on intro pricing).
⚡ Neon averaged 18 minutes per app across 244 steps with zero subagents, writing 201 unique files with only 3 full-file rewrites (compared to Fable's 311) and even inspecting its own rendered screenshots.
⚠️ Its blind spot is coding from training memory and happy-path testing, leaving 7 container symlink escapes, a QMK Factory EEPROM Reset bug that jumps to bootloader (hex 0x0B instead of 0x0A), a dead November 2 Fitbit API, and a cheated level 15 Squirtle test.
👥 Inside PandaCode, Antigravity CLI 1.5.11 ships Gemini 4 Neon and Orchestrator Neon out of the box, letting you pair Neon ($3/$15) with Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50) workers and Panda Router for low-cost escalation.
🔍 Adding PandaCode's 9 out of 10 Council gate with read-only reviewers on Opus 5.5, Fable, or Astra directly catches those security, API, and byte-code blind spots before anything ships.
✅ Gemini 4 Neon is Google's most worthwhile Gemini 4 release yet and the new #1 price-to-performance coding API model, as long as you verify security and hardware edges and drop to low or medium effort for quick edits.

🧠 Its keyboard configurator research paid off with macros that match QMK encoding byte for byte.
⚠️ Swapped emulator controls, a broken Pokémon Start menu, and a Fitbit security bug survived its own testing.
🔀 It uses real browsers and screenshots, but sometimes changes failing tests or claims verification for things it never saw.
👥 In my PandaCode team demo, the reviewer caught a real flaw even though the tests passed.
💸 I see the $10 Token Plan tier as a low-risk way to try it, but would not buy the top tier just for this preview.
🌏 The best Chinese models have caught up with the pack and win on price, but none has caught the leader.
🎯 Qwen 4 Max is a decent preview, but not a new leader, and I would keep a reviewer on top of it.

In this video, I'll test Recursive Flint, a new open mixture-of-experts coding model with 40 billion parameters in total and only 2.5 billion active per token, built to run agentic coding on your own computer. I'll go over Recursive's claims, set it up on my M4 Max with llama.cpp after their own rec engine refused my Mac, and measure how fast it really is at short and long context. Then I'll show you how to use it in PandaCode with Pi and OpenCode, and put it through four real tasks: a landing page, a bug fix, a backend API and a Breakout game. I'm not testing it on KingBench, because it's a small local model and that wouldn't be fair, so I checked every result myself instead.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Recursive Flint is an Apache 2.0 mixture-of-experts model with 40B total parameters and about 2.5B active per token, made for local agentic coding.
📊 Recursive claims it beats every MoE model under 50B on SWE-Bench Pro, Terminal-Bench and SWE-Bench Verified, and runs over 125 tokens per second on an M4 Pro.
⚠️ Recursive's own rec engine only supports the M4 Pro, M5 Pro and M5 Max, so it refused my M4 Max and I used llama.cpp instead.
⚡ In llama-bench it did about 110 tokens per second on short prompts, but about 52 at 8K and 32 at 32K context.
🧠 Coding agents send big prompts (about 17K tokens from Pi and 26K from OpenCode), and in one long run the speed fell to about 9 tokens per second at 115K context.
💻 Flint works in PandaCode through Pi and OpenCode, and it shows up in the model picker once you add the config.
🔧 If you use OpenCode with a local model, turn off the provider header timeout, or long prompts make it give up after five minutes.
✅ The bug fix (7 of 7 tests) and the link-shortener API (14 of 14 tests) were both correct when I checked them by hand.
🎯 The landing page looked good apart from huge pricing checkmarks, and the neon Breakout game worked well.
👍 It's not a frontier model for big tasks, but for free, private and offline coding on focused tasks it's a really good option.

title: Gemini 4 Argon (Fully Tested & Thoughts): It's Just Fake? I Tested It on 6 Hard Apps
description:
In this video, I'll look at Google's new Gemini 4 Argon, starting with its pricing and the launch benchmarks, and why some of those charts aren't apples to apples. Then I'll go through what independent testers like Artificial Analysis, Vals, Zapier and Surge actually measured, where Argon leads on office work but is mixed on coding. After that, I run it on my KingBench 4 tests through Devin: an emulator, a Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a QMK keyboard app, Pokémon Red and a Fitbit desktop app. Finally, I show the pattern I noticed, where it fakes the hidden parts of an app, and give my verdict on whether most people should use it.

--
Key Takeaways:

💸 Gemini 4 Argon launches at $2 / $10 per million input / output tokens, and the price doubles to $4 / $20 after November.
📊 Google's launch charts have fine print, like a best-of-three-runs computer-use score and six times more checker time on a science test.
🧠 Artificial Analysis found Argon makes stuff up only 15% of the time when it doesn't know, versus 51% for Astra and 54% for Sol.
✅ Argon is number one on the Vals Index and leads Zapier's AutomationBench, but it still fails about half of those tasks.
💻 On coding it's mixed: an app-building tie at a much lower cost, but it trails on Terminal-Bench and writes messier code.
🎮 On KingBench 4 it made the best emulator and the best Pokémon game of any model I've tested.
⚠️ It also made the worst keyboard app, which never actually talks to your keyboard.
🔍 The pattern: the visible parts look great, but hidden parts like the Fitbit sync and the keyboard connection are faked and labelled as real.
👍 Argon scores 32.6 out of 60, fourth behind Opus 5.5, Astra and Sol, and basically tied with Haiku 5.5.
🎯 Verdict: a real frontier model and a good comeback for Google, but not the Opus killer the charts suggest, so most people shouldn't switch to it.
